Growth trajectory analyses for the Mirror butterflyfish (Chaetodon speculum) indicate that individuals attain a maximum total length of 18 cm [Li = 18 cm], a size consistent with that of other medium-bodied corallivorous chaetodontids. Field surveys across the Indo-Pacific have documented that the onset of reproductive maturity occurs when individuals reach a total length of 6 cm [Lp = 6 cm], a threshold that corresponds to a wet body mass of approximately 5.3 grams [Wwp = approximately 5.3 grams] at puberty. The allometric relationship used to derive these mass estimates follows a standard length-weight power function commonly applied to butterflyfishes. Juveniles recruiting to reef habitats are notably small, with newly hatched larvae possessing a calculated wet weight at birth of 0.00023 grams [Wwb = 0.00023 grams], a value inferred from the average egg diameter of 0.75 mm recorded in the closely related congener Chaetodon larvatus. This minute initial mass reflects the pelagic spawning strategy typical of the genus, wherein small, buoyant eggs are released into the water column during broadcast spawning events.

The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of Chaetodon speculum provides a standardized metric of relative gonad mass. At a water temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], the gonadosomatic index was estimated at approximately 6% [GSI = approximately 6%]. The data, originally derived from comparative work on Chaetodon larvatus, imply that ovarian recrudescence and vitellogenesis proceed steadily under stable warm-water conditions. Spawning adults are believed to form monogamous pair bonds, a social structure that may necessitate frequent but energetically modest gamete releases to maintain pair cohesion and territorial defense over the extended breeding period typical of tropical chaetodontids.

The early life history of the Mirror butterflyfish is characterized by a brief embryonic period followed by a protracted pelagic larval phase. At a stable water temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], embryogenesis proceeds rapidly, with egg hatching occurring just 7 days [ab = 7 days] after fertilization, a duration that aligns with the fast developmental rates typical of tropical marine teleosts. The resulting yolk-sac larva is entirely lecithotrophic for a short window, relying on endogenous reserves before the mouth opens and the exotrophic transition begins. Pelagic teleost larvae then drift in ocean currents for several weeks, feeding on planktonic prey until they reach a developmental stage capable of sensing suitable benthic settlement cues. The ability to complete embryonic development in under a week at these temperatures allows for rapid turnover of spawning events, potentially enabling multiple reproductive cycles within a single breeding season and thereby buffering against stochastic variability in larval survival.

Longevity records for Chaetodon speculum suggest a maximum lifespan of approximately 7,300 days [am = approximately 7,300 days] when maintained at a thermal regime of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], a figure that approaches two decades in the wild. This extended lifespan is consistent with the slow life-history pace observed in many coral reef fishes, where stable environmental conditions and low natural mortality rates among adults favor delayed senescence. Field observations of tagged individuals in the Great Barrier Reef and the Coral Triangle have corroborated this estimate, with some recaptures occurring more than 15 years after initial marking. Senescent adult death in this species typically results from gradual physiological decline rather than acute predation, as adults benefit from strong territorial behaviors and protective spines.

Body mass at the adult asymptote for Chaetodon speculum reaches approximately 137.4 grams [Wwi = approximately 137.4 grams], derived from a length-weight regression based on the maximum total length of 18 centimeters. This ultimate wet weight places the species among the larger members of its genus, though still considerably smaller than some butterflyfishes that attain masses exceeding 300 grams. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows a steep power exponent, indicating that late-stage somatic growth involves substantial tissue accretion relative to linear extension. Post-settlement juveniles undergo a rapid phase of mass gain as they transition from a planktonic to a benthic diet, with the weight at puberty of 5.3 grams marking the point at which energy begins to be diverted from somatic growth toward gametogenesis. The allometric scaling between the mass at puberty and the asymptotic mass suggests that individuals allocate roughly 96 percent of their total growth trajectory to reaching reproductive size before further mass accumulation slows considerably in mature adults.
